## 83. Multi-Agent Decision Coordination

**Section ID:** `CAT-DE-P4-83`  
**Constitutional domain:** Multi-Agent Coordination Governance  
**Human accountable owner:** Lead Repository Architect and Documentation Owner  
**Primary record:** coordination session record  
**Decision status:** Foundation decision; evidence-gated. Later ADRs MUST preserve the behaviour specified here unless they explicitly supersede a named clause.  
**Primary question:** How do many agents coordinate one decision surface without collisions, impersonation, or unbudgeted drift, and how is every coordination session recorded?

### Purpose

This section extends Section 67 (`Multi-Agent Decision Runtime`) without rewriting it. Section 67 established the multi-agent runtime with recorded coordination and terminal human override; this section adds the coordination discipline: coordination sessions, role binding, turn protocols, coordination budgets, and collision detection. The central claim: coordination is a budgeted, recorded, role-bound session; agents that coordinate outside a session are not coordinating, they are colliding.

**Normative application:** For `Multi-Agent Decision Coordination`, the owning implementation MUST make this purpose observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Business Perspective

The business scales agents to scale decisions, and uncoordinated agents cost more than they save: duplicate work, contradictory outcomes, and untraceable responsibility. Coordination sessions give the business one record per joint effort — who participated, under which role, spending which budget — which turns agent collaboration into a reviewable production line instead of a chat room.

**Normative application:** For `Multi-Agent Decision Coordination`, the owning implementation MUST make this business outcome observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Engineering Perspective

Engineering models the coordination session as a typed record: session identifier, purpose, participant set with role bindings, turn protocol, budget, state, and receipts. Participation requires a bound role from the Section 51 registry; turns follow a declared protocol; budgets cap total agent spend per session; collision detection refuses two agents writing the same decision surface concurrently; and the session record is append-only.

**Normative application:** For `Multi-Agent Decision Coordination`, the owning implementation MUST make this engineering behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Architecture Perspective

Architecturally coordination is a protocol over the agent fabric port of Section 3: agents join sessions through the fabric, role binding comes from Section 51, authority ceilings from Section 52, and consensus needs flow to Section 84. The multi-agent runtime of Section 67 hosts the sessions; no new core enters the architecture.

**Normative application:** For `Multi-Agent Decision Coordination`, the owning implementation MUST make this architectural position observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### AI Perspective

For an AI collaborator coordination is where its improvisation instinct invents side channels. The characteristic AI failure is the out-of-band whisper: two agents coordinate in a private channel the record never sees. The obligations are mechanical: an AI coordinates only inside recorded sessions, under its bound role, within the session budget; it never shares decision-affecting information outside the session record.

**Normative application:** For `Multi-Agent Decision Coordination`, the owning implementation MUST make this agent behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Constitutional Controls

#### CAT-DE-P4-83-C01 — Sessions or silence

- **Control ID:** `CAT-DE-P4-83-C01`
- **Title:** Sessions or silence
- **Normative statement:** Decision-affecting coordination between agents MUST occur inside a recorded session; out-of-band coordination outcomes MUST be refused and re-run inside a session.
- **Security assertion:** An unrecorded channel is an unowned influence.
- **Evidence:** session records and gap detections.
- **Failure code:** `CAT_DE_P4_83_C01`
- **Recovery:** Re-run the outcome in a recorded session.
- **Implementation test:** Out-of-band coordination tests.
- **Ownership:** Coordination Owner

#### CAT-DE-P4-83-C02 — Roles bind before work

- **Control ID:** `CAT-DE-P4-83-C02`
- **Title:** Roles bind before work
- **Normative statement:** A participant without a bound Section 51 role MUST be refused at session admission.
- **Security assertion:** An unbound participant has no defined ceiling.
- **Evidence:** admission receipts.
- **Failure code:** `CAT_DE_P4_83_C02`
- **Recovery:** Bind the role and re-admit.
- **Implementation test:** Unbound role tests.
- **Ownership:** Coordination Owner
- **Constitutional assertion:** This control is binding for `Multi-Agent Decision Coordination` and MUST NOT be weakened without a superseding ADR.

#### CAT-DE-P4-83-C03 — One writer per surface

- **Control ID:** `CAT-DE-P4-83-C03`
- **Title:** One writer per surface
- **Normative statement:** Concurrent writes to one decision surface MUST be refused; the surface has exactly one writer at a time.
- **Security assertion:** Concurrent writers corrupt the record they share.
- **Evidence:** collision refusal records.
- **Failure code:** `CAT_DE_P4_83_C03`

- **Implementation test:** Write collision tests.
- **Ownership:** Coordination Owner
- **Constitutional assertion:** This control is binding for `Multi-Agent Decision Coordination` and MUST NOT be weakened without a superseding ADR.

### Constitutional Rule

#### CAT-DE-CONST-084 — Recorded coordination

- **Rule ID:** `CAT-DE-CONST-084`
- **Title:** Recorded coordination
- **Purpose:** To keep every joint agent effort session-recorded, role-bound, collision-free, and budgeted.
- **Scope:** All coordination sessions, participants, turns, and budgets.
- **Normative statement:** Joint efforts MUST run in recorded sessions, participants MUST bind roles at admission, one writer per decision surface MUST hold, and sessions MUST stay inside declared budgets.
- **Rationale:** Collaboration without a record is collusion without a name; parallel writers without a lock are corruption with a schedule.
- **Enforcement point:** Session admission and turn paths.
- **Violation behavior:** The admission, write, or spend is refused with the violated clause named.
- **Validation method:** Session, role, collision, and budget tests.
- **Owner:** Coordination Owner
- **Related concepts:** Multi-Agent Decision Runtime, Decision Agent Roles, Decision Consensus, Decision Economics
- **Failure Condition:** Out-of-band coordination influences a decision, a roleless agent participates, or a surface has two writers.
- **Recovery:** Re-run in a session; bind the role; serialize the writers.

**Normative application:** For `Multi-Agent Decision Coordination`, the owning implementation MUST make this rule observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Pseudo Code

```text
function admit_participant(session, agent):
    if not ROLES.bound(agent):
        return refuse("role_unbound", agent.id)
    session.participants.append(bind(agent, ROLES.role_of(agent)))
    return session
```

## 84. Consensus and Dissent

**Section ID:** `CAT-DE-P4-84`  
**Constitutional domain:** Decision Consensus Governance  
**Human accountable owner:** Lead Repository Architect and Documentation Owner  
**Primary record:** consensus record  
**Decision status:** Foundation decision; evidence-gated. Later ADRs MUST preserve the behaviour specified here unless they explicitly supersede a named clause.  
**Primary question:** How does consensus form, how is dissent captured and preserved, how are quorums computed and ties broken, and when does consensus fail upward?

### Purpose

This section extends Section 54 (`Decision Consensus`) without rewriting it. Section 54 established eight consensus strategies with quorum, timeout, abstention, and verbatim minority reports; this section adds the operational consensus discipline: quorum mathematics, weighted voting recall, tie-breaking rules, dissent preservation, and fail-upward paths. The central claim: consensus is a recorded agreement that preserves its dissent; a consensus that erases disagreement is a vote with the minority deleted, and that is not consensus, that is fiction.

**Normative application:** For `Consensus and Dissent`, the owning implementation MUST make this purpose observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Business Perspective

The business uses consensus where a wrong decision is costlier than a slow one. The value of dissent preservation is retrospective: when a consensus decision fails, the minority report explains what the majority dismissed, which converts every failure into a reviewable lesson instead of a mystery. Fail-upward paths guarantee that deadlock costs time, not operations.

**Normative application:** For `Consensus and Dissent`, the owning implementation MUST make this business outcome observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Engineering Perspective

Engineering models the consensus record as a typed outcome: consensus identifier, strategy, participant set with weights, quorum requirement, votes cast, abstentions, tie-break rule applied, majority verdict, and the verbatim minority report. Quorum is computed from declared weights; a tie applies the declared tie-break without discretion; dissent is stored verbatim, unedited; and failure to reach quorum or consensus within the timeout fails upward to arbitration of Section 82 or the human gate of Section 85.

**Normative application:** For `Consensus and Dissent`, the owning implementation MUST make this engineering behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Architecture Perspective

Architecturally consensus is a protocol over the coordination sessions of Section 83: participants vote inside a recorded session, votes carry the Section 55 weighted voting envelope, and the outcome feeds the decision record. The consensus runtime of Section 54 hosts the strategies; this section binds their operational rules.

**Normative application:** For `Consensus and Dissent`, the owning implementation MUST make this architectural position observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### AI Perspective

For an AI collaborator consensus is where its harmony instinct suppresses disagreement. The characteristic AI failure is dissent smoothing: the model paraphrases the minority into agreement so the record looks unanimous. The obligations are mechanical: an AI records dissent verbatim, never paraphrases it into agreement, applies tie-breaks by the declared rule only, and reports failure to reach consensus as failure, never as a softer verdict.

**Normative application:** For `Consensus and Dissent`, the owning implementation MUST make this agent behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

- Declaring consensus without quorum.

### Best Practices

- Record dissent verbatim and immutable.
- Compute quorum from declared weights.
- Apply declared tie-breaks mechanically.

### Constitutional Rule

#### CAT-DE-CONST-085 — Dissent preserved

- **Rule ID:** `CAT-DE-CONST-085`
- **Title:** Dissent preserved
- **Purpose:** To keep every consensus quorum-bound, dissent-verbatim, tie-declared, and fail-upward.
- **Scope:** All consensus rounds, votes, quorums, ties, and dissent records.
- **Normative statement:** Consensus verdicts MUST meet the computed weighted quorum, MUST preserve dissent verbatim and immutable, MUST break ties by declared rules only, and MUST fail upward at timeout to arbitration or the human gate.
- **Rationale:** A consensus system that erases its minority is a majority machine; a deadlock that never resolves is a stall machine.
- **Enforcement point:** Tally, tie, and timeout paths.
- **Violation behavior:** The verdict, tie, or dissent edit is refused with the violated clause named.
- **Validation method:** Quorum, dissent, tie, and timeout tests.
- **Owner:** Consensus Owner
- **Related concepts:** Decision Consensus, Decision Voting, Decision Arbitration, Decision Human-in-the-Loop
- **Failure Condition:** A verdict lacks quorum, dissent is edited, a tie breaks by preference, or a deadlock hides.
- **Recovery:** Refuse the verdict; restore the dissent; apply the declared rule; fail upward.

**Normative application:** For `Consensus and Dissent`, the owning implementation MUST make this rule observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Pseudo Code

```text
function tally(round):
    quorum = QUORUM.compute(round.participants)
    if round.votes_cast < quorum:
        return refuse("quorum_not_met", round.id)
    verdict = TALLY.count(round.votes)
    if verdict.is_tie():
        verdict = TIES.apply(round.tie_break_rule, round.votes)
    DISSENT.store_verbatim(round.minority_reports)
    return verdict
```

## 85. Human-in-the-Loop Decisions

**Section ID:** `CAT-DE-P4-85`  
**Constitutional domain:** Human Gate Governance  
**Human accountable owner:** Lead Repository Architect and Documentation Owner  
**Primary record:** human review record  
**Decision status:** Foundation decision; evidence-gated. Later ADRs MUST preserve the behaviour specified here unless they explicitly supersede a named clause.  
**Primary question:** How do human approval, rejection, and escalation work, how are review SLAs enforced, and how is the human gate protected from spoofing?

### Purpose

This section extends Section 59 (`Decision Human-in-the-Loop`) without rewriting it. Section 59 established human gates that automation may feed but never pass; this section adds the operational gate discipline: human approval and rejection records, human escalation, review SLAs, spoofing protection, and the audit of human actions. The central claim: the human gate is the terminal authority crossing, and it is protected in both directions — automation cannot pass it, and nothing can fake the human on the other side.

**Normative application:** For `Human-in-the-Loop Decisions`, the owning implementation MUST make this purpose observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Business Perspective

The business stakes its risk appetite on humans holding the highest-impact decisions. Every human action at the gate must therefore be a recorded, attributable, timely act: the approval that opened a market, the rejection that blocked a campaign, the escalation that pulled a decision up a level. Review SLAs keep gates from becoming bottlenecks; spoofing protection keeps them from becoming theater.

**Normative application:** For `Human-in-the-Loop Decisions`, the owning implementation MUST make this business outcome observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Engineering Perspective

Engineering models the human review record as a typed act: review identifier, decision identifier, human identity, role authority, action (approve, reject, escalate, request evidence), reason, timestamp, and SLA state. Approval and rejection are recorded with reasons; escalation moves the decision up the authority ladder; review SLAs alert on stale reviews; spoofing protection binds human identities to verified credentials; and the gate refuses any act whose identity or authority fails verification.

**Normative application:** For `Human-in-the-Loop Decisions`, the owning implementation MUST make this engineering behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Architecture Perspective

Architecturally the human gate is a port discipline: the gate port of Section 3 is the only crossing where a human credential can authorize a decision action, and the gate itself is a Section 22 component. Automation may present evidence to the gate; only a verified human credential may act at it. No architectural change is introduced; the gate is made unforgeable.

**Normative application:** For `Human-in-the-Loop Decisions`, the owning implementation MUST make this architectural position observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### AI Perspective

For an AI collaborator the human gate is where its helpfulness instinct impersonates the human. The characteristic AI failure is gate theater: the model writes "human approved" on its own output because the human would have approved. The obligations are mechanical: an AI never performs or fabricates a human act, never signs a review it did not witness, treats the gate as closed until a verified human act opens it, and escalates to a human when the gate is stale instead of waiting silently.

**Normative application:** For `Human-in-the-Loop Decisions`, the owning implementation MUST make this agent behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Constitutional Rule

#### CAT-DE-CONST-086 — Automation never passes the gate

- **Rule ID:** `CAT-DE-CONST-086`
- **Title:** Automation never passes the gate
- **Purpose:** To keep the human gate credential-bound, recorded, SLA-enforced, and spoof-proof in both directions.
- **Scope:** All gate crossings, human acts, review SLAs, and escalations.
- **Normative statement:** The gate MUST open only to verified human acts recording identity, authority, action, and reason; synthetic and replayed acts MUST refuse; stale reviews MUST escalate within their SLA; and the audit trail MUST be append-only.
- **Rationale:** The gate exists because some decisions are human's alone; a forgeable gate is a risk appetite with a hole in it.
- **Enforcement point:** Gate admission and review paths.
- **Violation behavior:** The act is refused with the violated clause named and alerted.
- **Validation method:** Credential, record, SLA, and trail tests.
- **Owner:** Gate Policy Owner
- **Related concepts:** Decision Human-in-the-Loop, Decision Autonomy Boundaries, Decision Escalation, Decision Governance
- **Failure Condition:** A synthetic or replayed act passes, a gate rots, or an act goes unrecorded.
- **Recovery:** Refuse and alert; escalate the stale gate; record the act.

**Normative application:** For `Human-in-the-Loop Decisions`, the owning implementation MUST make this rule observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Pseudo Code

```text
function act_at_gate(act):
    if not CREDENTIALS.verify(act.human_identity, act.signature):
        return refuse("synthetic_human_act", act.id)
    if REPLAYS.seen(act.signature):
        return refuse("replayed_human_act", act.id)
    if not act.complete():
        return refuse("act_incomplete", act.id)
    REVIEWS.append(act)
    return act
```

## 86. Decision Escalation

**Section ID:** `CAT-DE-P4-86`  
**Constitutional domain:** Decision Escalation Governance  
**Human accountable owner:** Lead Repository Architect and Documentation Owner  
**Primary record:** escalation record  
**Decision status:** Foundation decision; evidence-gated. Later ADRs MUST preserve the behaviour specified here unless they explicitly supersede a named clause.  
**Primary question:** How does escalation climb the authority ladder, how are escalation TTLs and budgets enforced, and where does escalation terminate?

### Purpose

This section defines the escalation discipline: the escalation ladder, escalation records, escalation TTLs, escalation budgets, regional escalation, and the terminal human rung. Its central claim: escalation is the engine's way of saying "this decision exceeds what I am allowed to hold"; it is bounded in time and spend, it climbs deterministically, and it always terminates at a human — escalation that circulates forever is a failure loop, not a process.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Escalation`, the owning implementation MUST make this purpose observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Business Perspective

The business needs problems to climb to the right level quickly and to stop climbing when they arrive. Escalation TTLs prevent decisions from lingering at intermediate rungs; budgets prevent escalation from becoming an infinite cost; the terminal human rung guarantees that every escalation ends with a responsible person, which is what makes the whole autonomy model palatable to auditors and boards.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Escalation`, the owning implementation MUST make this business outcome observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Engineering Perspective

Engineering models the escalation record as a typed climb: escalation identifier, decision identifier, trigger, current rung, ladder definition, TTL per rung, total budget, history of rungs, and terminal state. Each rung has a declared TTL; expiry climbs to the next rung; the total budget caps the climb; the terminal rung is a human role from Section 51; and every climb writes an append-only history entry.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Escalation`, the owning implementation MUST make this engineering behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Architecture Perspective

Architecturally escalation is a policy over the authority model of Section 52: each rung is an authority level, the ladder is the ordered levels, and the terminal rung is the human supervisor role. Escalation exercises the authority core and the human gate of Section 85; it adds no new component.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Escalation`, the owning implementation MUST make this architectural position observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### AI Perspective

For an AI collaborator escalation is where its independence instinct withholds problems. The characteristic AI failure is the silent hold: the model sits on a decision it cannot authorize because escalating feels like failure. The obligations are mechanical: an AI escalates the moment a decision exceeds its authority, records the trigger, respects rung TTLs and budgets, and never circulates an escalation past its terminal rung.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Escalation`, the owning implementation MUST make this agent behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

- **Title:** Excess always climbs

### Constitutional Rule

#### CAT-DE-CONST-087 — Bounded escalation

- **Rule ID:** `CAT-DE-CONST-087`
- **Title:** Bounded escalation
- **Purpose:** To keep every escalation immediate, TTL-bounded, budget-capped, and human-terminated.
- **Scope:** All escalation ladders, rungs, triggers, and budgets.
- **Normative statement:** Authority-exceeded decisions MUST escalate immediately, every rung MUST carry a TTL, loops MUST jump to the human rung, climbs MUST stay inside declared budgets, and every ladder MUST terminate at a human rung.
- **Rationale:** Escalation exists to hand problems upward; an unbounded or circulating escalation is a problem that learned to hide.
- **Enforcement point:** Trigger, climb, and budget paths.
- **Violation behavior:** The hold, climb, or spend is refused with the violated clause named.
- **Validation method:** Trigger, TTL, loop, and budget tests.
- **Owner:** Escalation Owner
- **Related concepts:** Decision Agent Authority, Decision Human-in-the-Loop, Decision Failure Handling, Decision Governance
- **Failure Condition:** A hold is silent, a climb loops, or a budget is exceeded.
- **Recovery:** Fire the trigger; jump to the human rung; halt and alert.

### Pseudo Code

```text
function climb(escalation):
    next_rung = escalation.next_rung()
    if escalation.history.contains(next_rung):
        return jump_to_terminal(escalation, "escalation_loop")
    if escalation.budget.spent >= escalation.budget.limit:
        return halt("escalation_budget_exhausted", escalation.id)
    return ESCALATION_RECORDS.handoff(escalation, next_rung)
```

## 87. Decision Recovery

**Section ID:** `CAT-DE-P4-87`  
**Constitutional domain:** Decision Recovery Governance  
**Human accountable owner:** Lead Repository Architect and Documentation Owner  
**Primary record:** decision recovery record  
**Decision status:** Foundation decision; evidence-gated. Later ADRs MUST preserve the behaviour specified here unless they explicitly supersede a named clause.  
**Primary question:** How do rollback, compensation, checkpoint restore, and region failover recover decisions, and why is recovery always restore-only?

### Purpose

This section extends Section 47 (`Decision Recovery`) without rewriting it. Section 47 established the restore-only recovery ladder; this section adds the operational recovery discipline: rollback of decided outcomes, compensation for partially applied flows, checkpoint restore, recovery playbooks, and region failover. The central claim: recovery restores history, it never rewrites it — the engine heals by going back to a recorded point, never by editing the record of what went wrong.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Recovery`, the owning implementation MUST make this purpose observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Business Perspective

The business survives failures through recovery: a wrong price rolls back, a half-applied campaign compensates, a lost region fails over. Restore-only recovery is the business's guarantee that failures are visible and reversible: every recovery is itself recorded, so the story of what failed and how it was fixed survives for auditors and for the learning loops of Section 90.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Recovery`, the owning implementation MUST make this business outcome observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Engineering Perspective

Engineering models the recovery record as a typed act: recovery identifier, failure reference, recovery type (rollback, compensation, checkpoint restore, failover), checkpoint reference, steps applied, and state. Rollback restores the pre-decision state of the affected records; compensation applies the reverse steps of Section 78; checkpoint restore rewinds to a validated checkpoint; region failover re-homes shard work to a surviving region. Every recovery act is append-only evidence, never an edit.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Recovery`, the owning implementation MUST make this engineering behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Architecture Perspective

Architecturally recovery rides the repository runtime of Section 24: checkpoints are repository checkpoints, rollback is repository rollback, and failover is shard re-homing under the shard map of Section 76. Recovery adds no new core; it binds the existing repository and shard machinery to a discipline.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Recovery`, the owning implementation MUST make this architectural position observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### AI Perspective

For an AI collaborator recovery is where its repair instinct edits history to look fixed. The characteristic AI failure is the cleanup edit: the model silently corrects the wrong record instead of rolling it back visibly. The obligations are mechanical: an AI recovers by recorded restore-only acts, applies playbooks in their declared order, and never edits the failed record to erase the failure.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Recovery`, the owning implementation MUST make this agent behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Constitutional Controls

#### CAT-DE-P4-87-C01 — Never edit the failed record

- **Control ID:** `CAT-DE-P4-87-C01`
- **Title:** Never edit the failed record
- **Normative statement:** Recovery MUST NOT edit the failed record; cleanup edits MUST be refused and reverted.
- **Security assertion:** An edited failure is history rewritten to a preferred ending.
- **Evidence:** restore-only checks.
- **Failure code:** `CAT_DE_P4_87_C01`
- **Recovery:** Revert the edit and apply the declared playbook.
- **Implementation test:** Cleanup edit tests.
- **Ownership:** Recovery Owner
- **Constitutional assertion:** This control is binding for `Decision Recovery` and MUST NOT be weakened without a superseding ADR.

#### CAT-DE-P4-87-C02 — Checkpoints validate first

- **Control ID:** `CAT-DE-P4-87-C02`
- **Title:** Checkpoints validate first
- **Normative statement:** A checkpoint MUST validate before restore; an invalid checkpoint MUST fall back to the previous validated checkpoint.
- **Security assertion:** Restoring from a corrupted checkpoint imports the corruption.
- **Evidence:** checkpoint validation receipts.
- **Failure code:** `CAT_DE_P4_87_C02`
- **Recovery:** Fall back and re-validate.
- **Implementation test:** Invalid checkpoint tests.
- **Ownership:** Recovery Owner
- **Constitutional assertion:** This control is binding for `Decision Recovery` and MUST NOT be weakened without a superseding ADR.

#### CAT-DE-P4-87-C03 — Playbooks or refusal

- **Control ID:** `CAT-DE-P4-87-C03`
- **Title:** Playbooks or refusal
- **Normative statement:** A recovery without a declared playbook MUST be refused.
- **Security assertion:** Improvised recovery is a second failure wearing a fix.
- **Evidence:** playbook references per recovery.
- **Failure code:** `CAT_DE_P4_87_C03`
- **Recovery:** Declare the playbook and re-run.
- **Implementation test:** Missing playbook tests.
- **Ownership:** Recovery Owner
- **Constitutional assertion:** This control is binding for `Decision Recovery` and MUST NOT be weakened without a superseding ADR.

### Constitutional Rule

#### CAT-DE-CONST-088 — Restore-only recovery

- **Rule ID:** `CAT-DE-CONST-088`
- **Title:** Restore-only recovery
- **Purpose:** To keep every recovery a recorded, playbook-driven, validated, restore-only act.
- **Scope:** All rollbacks, compensations, checkpoint restores, and failovers.
- **Normative statement:** Recovery MUST be restore-only, MUST follow declared playbooks, MUST write append-only records, and MUST validate checkpoints before restore.
- **Rationale:** The engine's history is its most valuable asset; recovery that edits it trades the asset for a moment of tidiness.
- **Enforcement point:** Recovery admission and apply paths.
- **Violation behavior:** The recovery act is refused with the violated clause named.
- **Validation method:** Edit, playbook, record, and checkpoint tests.
- **Owner:** Recovery Owner
- **Related concepts:** Decision Recovery, Decision Orchestration, Decision Failure Handling, Decision Repository Runtime
- **Failure Condition:** A failed record is edited, a recovery is improvised, or a checkpoint restores unvalidated.
- **Recovery:** Revert the edit; declare the playbook; fall back to the previous checkpoint.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Recovery`, the owning implementation MUST make this rule observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Acceptance Tests

**Test ID:** `CAT-DE-AT-S87-001`  
**Purpose:** Cleanup edits refuse

**When:** the restore-only check runs  
**Then:** the edit refuses with `recovery_edit`

### Pseudo Code

```text
function recover(failure):
    playbook = PLAYBOOKS.for_class(failure.class)
    if not playbook:
        return refuse("playbook_missing", failure.id)
    for step in playbook.steps:
        RECOVERY_RECORDS.apply(step, failure)
    return RECOVERY_RECORDS.close(failure)
```

## 88. Decision Failure Handling

**Section ID:** `CAT-DE-P4-88`  
**Constitutional domain:** Decision Failure Governance  
**Human accountable owner:** Lead Repository Architect and Documentation Owner  
**Primary record:** failure incident record  
**Decision status:** Foundation decision; evidence-gated. Later ADRs MUST preserve the behaviour specified here unless they explicitly supersede a named clause.  
**Primary question:** How are partial and distributed failures, stale evidence and context, and the five drift families classified, contained, and learned from?

### Purpose

This section defines the failure handling discipline: failure classification, partial failure, distributed failure, stale evidence, stale context, and the five drift families — decision drift, policy drift, goal drift, model drift, and agent drift. Its central claim: failures are typed, contained, and recorded events; the engine treats a failure as data for the learning loops of Section 90, not as a secret to bury.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Failure Handling`, the owning implementation MUST make this purpose observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Business Perspective

The business measures the engine by how failures behave: a contained failure costs one decision; an uncontained one costs a day. Failure classification gives the business a shared vocabulary for incidents, and drift detection converts slow degradations — a policy drifting, a model drifting, an agent drifting — into visible, owned problems before they become silent changes in business behavior.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Failure Handling`, the owning implementation MUST make this business outcome observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Engineering Perspective

Engineering models the failure incident record as a typed event: incident identifier, failure class (partial, distributed, stale evidence, stale context, drift family), detection signal, blast radius, containment action, accountable owner, and state. Partial failures isolate to the affected shard; distributed failures quorum through the coordination of Section 83; stale evidence and context refuse at the freshness gates of Sections 8 and 7; each drift family has a detector, a threshold, and a remediation path.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Failure Handling`, the owning implementation MUST make this engineering behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Architecture Perspective

Architecturally failure handling is the negative-space discipline of the whole document: the freshness gates of Sections 7 and 8 catch staleness, the isolation of Section 61 catches partial failures, the consensus of Section 84 catches distributed disagreement, and the drift detectors sit over the analytics of Section 90. Failure handling adds no new core; it names and binds the existing gates.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Failure Handling`, the owning implementation MUST make this architectural position observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### AI Perspective

For an AI collaborator failure handling is where its pride instinct hides errors. The characteristic AI failure is the silent retry spiral: the model retries a failing decision endlessly because admitting failure feels worse. The obligations are mechanical: an AI classifies and records failures honestly, contains them at their blast radius, and stops retrying past the declared limit — the retry budget exists precisely so that failure is finite.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Failure Handling`, the owning implementation MUST make this agent behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Constitutional Controls

#### CAT-DE-P4-88-C01 — No retry spirals

- **Control ID:** `CAT-DE-P4-88-C01`
- **Title:** No retry spirals
- **Normative statement:** A decision whose retries exhaust the declared budget MUST fail finite and record; further retries MUST refuse.
- **Security assertion:** An unbounded retry is a cost with no ceiling and a failure with no record.
- **Evidence:** retry budget receipts.
- **Failure code:** `CAT_DE_P4_88_C01`
- **Recovery:** Record the incident and hand to Section 87 recovery.
- **Implementation test:** Retry spiral tests.
- **Ownership:** Failure Handling Owner
- **Constitutional assertion:** This control is binding for `Decision Failure Handling` and MUST NOT be weakened without a superseding ADR.

#### CAT-DE-P4-88-C02 — Stale inputs never decide

- **Control ID:** `CAT-DE-P4-88-C02`
- **Title:** Stale inputs never decide
- **Normative statement:** Evidence or context past its freshness window MUST be refused before evaluation.
- **Security assertion:** A decision on stale data is a decision about a world that no longer exists.
- **Evidence:** freshness gate receipts.
- **Failure code:** `CAT_DE_P4_88_C02`
- **Recovery:** Re-fetch the input or reopen the decision.
- **Implementation test:** Stale input tests.
- **Ownership:** Decision Owner
- **Constitutional assertion:** This control is binding for `Decision Failure Handling` and MUST NOT be weakened without a superseding ADR.

#### CAT-DE-P4-88-C03 — Every drift family detected

- **Control ID:** `CAT-DE-P4-88-C03`
- **Title:** Every drift family detected
- **Normative statement:** Decision, policy, goal, model, and agent drift MUST each have a detector with a declared threshold and remediation path.
- **Security assertion:** Undetected drift is silent behavior change wearing a version number.
- **Evidence:** detector registration and alert records.
- **Failure code:** `CAT_DE_P4_88_C03`
- **Recovery:** Remediate via the declared path and record.
- **Implementation test:** Drift detector coverage tests.
- **Ownership:** Drift Detector Owner
- **Constitutional assertion:** This control is binding for `Decision Failure Handling` and MUST NOT be weakened without a superseding ADR.

### Constitutional Rule

#### CAT-DE-CONST-089 — Contained failure

- **Rule ID:** `CAT-DE-CONST-089`
- **Title:** Contained failure
- **Purpose:** To keep every failure classified, contained, recorded, staleness-refused, retry-bounded, and drift-detected.
- **Scope:** All failure incidents, staleness gates, retries, and drift detectors.
- **Normative statement:** Failures MUST classify and record before containment, stale evidence and context MUST refuse at the freshness gates, retry budgets MUST make failure finite, and every drift family MUST hold a thresholded detector with a remediation path.
- **Rationale:** A failure the engine cannot see, bound, or learn from is not a failure; it is a liability with a retry loop.
- **Enforcement point:** Failure, retry, and staleness paths.
- **Violation behavior:** The retry, input, or incident is refused with the violated clause named.
- **Validation method:** Incident, staleness, retry, and drift tests.
- **Owner:** Failure Handling Owner
- **Related concepts:** Decision Recovery, Decision Analytics, Decision Observability, Decision Isolation
- **Failure Condition:** A retry spirals, a stale input decides, or a drift family goes undetected.
- **Recovery:** Bound the retries; re-fetch the input; register the detector and remediate.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Failure Handling`, the owning implementation MUST make this rule observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Pseudo Code

```text
function handle_failure(failure):
    if failure.retries_used >= failure.retry_budget.limit:
        INCIDENTS.record(failure, state="contained")
        return RECOVERY.handoff(failure)
    if STALENESS.is_stale(failure.inputs):
        return refuse("input_stale", failure.inputs)
    return RETRIES.attempt(failure)
```

## 89. Decision Integration

**Section ID:** `CAT-DE-P4-89`  
**Constitutional domain:** Decision Integration Governance  
**Human accountable owner:** Lead Repository Architect and Documentation Owner  
**Primary record:** integration contract record  
**Decision status:** Foundation decision; evidence-gated. Later ADRs MUST preserve the behaviour specified here unless they explicitly supersede a named clause.  
**Primary question:** How does the Decision Engine integrate with reasoning, planning, runtime, execution, memory, knowledge, governance, observability, agents, and repositories — and what makes each integration contractual rather than incidental?

### Purpose

This section defines the ten integration contracts of the Decision Engine: Reasoning → Decision, Planning → Decision, Decision → Runtime, Decision → Execution, Decision → Memory, Decision → Knowledge, Decision → Governance, Decision → Observability, Decision → Agent, and Decision → Repository. It extends the contracts of Sections 32 through 39 and Section 49 without rewriting them. Its central claim: every cross-engine communication is a versioned, traced, audited, idempotent contract with a security boundary; anything else is two systems sharing a database and calling it integration.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Integration`, the owning implementation MUST make this purpose observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Business Perspective

The business runs the engines as one product, and integrations are where the product lives or dies. A versioned integration means one engine can evolve without breaking the others; a traced integration means a decision can be reconstructed across all ten boundaries; an audited integration means the business can answer "which engine knew what, when" for any outcome. Integration contracts are the business's insurance policy for a multi-engine architecture.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Integration`, the owning implementation MUST make this business outcome observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Engineering Perspective

Engineering models each integration as a typed contract record: purpose, contract identifier, input and output schemas, authority requirement, validation rules, failure behavior, timeout, retry policy, idempotency key derivation, correlation and trace identifiers, audit record format, security boundary, versioning, compatibility window, and recovery path. Every integration validates its inputs at the port, fails into a declared behavior, retries within a budget, and records an audit line that binds all identifiers.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Integration`, the owning implementation MUST make this engineering behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Architecture Perspective

Architecturally the integrations ride the eight ports of Section 3: no integration invents a side door. Each engine communicates only through its declared ports, so the port contracts of this section are the whole integration surface — which is what makes the multi-engine CAT architecture composable instead of entangled.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Integration`, the owning implementation MUST make this architectural position observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### AI Perspective

For an AI collaborator integrations are where its convenience instinct invents side channels. The characteristic AI failure is the direct read: the model queries another engine's store directly because the contract felt slow. The obligations are mechanical: an AI communicates only through declared contracts, validates inputs and outputs at the port, and treats a contract version change as a governed event, never as a private adjustment.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Integration`, the owning implementation MUST make this agent behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Integration Contracts

#### Integration: Reasoning → Decision

| Aspect | Value |
|---|---|
| Purpose | Carry reasoning evidence and recommendations into decision evaluation without making them decisions. |
| Contract | `DE-INT-REASONING-01` — the reasoning output contract, version 1.2.0. |
| Input | A reasoning verdict record from `context/09_REASONING_ENGINE.md` with source, evidence chain, confidence, and uncertainty bands. |
| Output | A decision evidence entry in the Section 8 evidence model, stamped with its reasoning provenance. |
| Authority | The reasoning engine may propose; only the Decision Engine selects. Confidence is evidence about uncertainty, never authorization. |
| Validation | The evidence admission rules of Section 8: source bound, freshness checked, exclusions recorded. |
| Failure behavior | Invalid reasoning input refuses at the evidence gate with `reasoning_evidence_invalid`. |
| Timeout | Target of 2 seconds for a reasoning query. |
| Retry | Budget of 2 retries with exponential backoff. |
| Idempotency | Keyed by reasoning verdict identifier; re-delivery deduplicates. |
| Correlation ID | `corr_de_<decision_id>` propagated into every evidence entry. |
| Trace ID | `trace_reasoning_<verdict_id>` spans the reasoning-to-decision hop. |
| Audit record | `decision_evidence_admitted` with verdict, decision, and gate receipts. |
| Security boundary | The reasoning port authenticates the peer; reasoning output never bypasses evidence admission. |
| Versioning | Contract versions in the integration registry; both engines announce changes. |
| Compatibility | One-version-back compatibility window; a breaking change requires a dual-read window. |
| Recovery | Refused evidence re-fetches or reopens the decision per Section 88. |

```text
function reasoning_to_decision(verdict):
    if not REASONING_PORT.authenticated(verdict.sender):
        return refuse("peer_unauthenticated", verdict.id)
    if not EVIDENCE_GATE.admit(verdict):
        return refuse("reasoning_evidence_invalid", verdict.id)
    return EVIDENCE.store(verdict.as_evidence(), verdict.provenance)
```

#### Integration: Planning → Decision

| Aspect | Value |
|---|---|
| Purpose | Carry goals, objectives, tasks, dependencies, constraints, resources, capacities, and timelines into decision evaluation. |
| Contract | `DE-INT-PLANNING-01` — the planning output contract, version 2.0.0, extending Sections 32 through 39. |
| Input | Planning bridge records from `context/11_PLANNING_ENGINE.md`: goal, objective, task, dependency, constraint, resource, capacity, timeline. |
| Output | Decision context bindings and constraint entries consumed by the pipeline of Section 21. |
| Authority | The Planning Engine plans; the Decision Engine decides. The Decision Engine MUST NOT silently mutate Planning Engine state. |
| Validation | Bridge schema validation per Section 32 through 39 mapping rules. |
| Failure behavior | A bridge record failing validation refuses with `planning_bridge_invalid`. |
| Timeout | Target of 2 seconds for a bridge query. |
| Retry | Budget of 2 retries with backoff. |
| Idempotency | Keyed by bridge record identifier. |
| Correlation ID | `corr_de_<decision_id>` binds the plan and the decision. |
| Trace ID | `trace_planning_<record_id>` spans the planning-to-decision hop. |
| Audit record | `planning_bridge_consumed` with record, decision, and validation receipts. |
| Security boundary | The planning port authenticates the peer; bridge records never carry execution authority. |
| Versioning | Contract versions in the integration registry. |
| Compatibility | One-version-back window with dual-read for breaking changes. |
| Recovery | Refused bridges re-fetch or reopen per Section 88. |

```text
function planning_to_decision(bridge):
    if not PLANNING_PORT.authenticated(bridge.sender):
        return refuse("peer_unauthenticated", bridge.id)
    if not BRIDGES.validate(bridge):
        return refuse("planning_bridge_invalid", bridge.id)
    return CONTEXT.bind(bridge.as_binding())
```

```text
function decision_to_runtime(decision):
    assembly = ASSEMBLIES.for(decision.assembly_id)
    if not assembly.verified():
        return refuse("assembly_refused", decision.id)
    return RUNTIME.run(decision, assembly)
```

#### Integration: Decision → Execution

| Timeout | Target of 30 seconds for a receipt. |
| Retry | Budget of 2 retries by idempotency key. |
| Idempotency | Keyed by idempotency key; duplicates return the original receipt. |

| Trace ID | `trace_execution_<intent_id>` spans the execution hop. |
| Audit record | `intent_emitted` and `receipt_bound` records. |
| Security boundary | The execution port is intent-only and authenticated in both directions. |
| Versioning | Contract versions in the integration registry. |
| Compatibility | One-version-back window; receipt binding is mandatory in every version. |
| Recovery | Missing receipts re-query by idempotency key per Section 77. |

| Purpose | Read and append decision records through the repository runtime. |
| Contract | `DE-INT-REPOSITORY-01` — the repository contract, version 1.0.0, per Section 24. |
| Input | A read query or an append request for a decision record. |
| Output | A query result or an append receipt with offset. |
| Authority | The repository runtime is the only reader and writer of the decision store. |
| Validation | Tenant scoping and record hash validation on every operation. |
| Failure behavior | A failed append refuses the lifecycle advance with `repository_append_failed`. |
| Timeout | Target of 2 seconds per operation. |
| Retry | Budget of 3 retries with backoff. |
| Idempotency | Keyed by record hash for appends; reads are naturally idempotent. |
| Correlation ID | `corr_de_<decision_id>` on every operation. |
| Trace ID | `trace_repository_<decision_id>` spans the operation. |
| Audit record | `repository_operation` with tenant, offset, and digest. |
| Security boundary | The repository port enforces tenant isolation and append-only writes. |
| Versioning | Contract versions in the integration registry. |
| Compatibility | One-version-back window; the append-only rule is invariant across versions. |
| Recovery | Failed appends retry by hash; the record is never half-written. |

```text
function decision_to_repository(op):
    if not op.tenant_scoped():
        return refuse("tenant_scope_missing", op.id)
    if op.is_append() and not op.hash_valid():
        return refuse("record_hash_invalid", op.id)
    return REPOSITORY.run(op)
```

### Security

Every integration authenticates its peer; inputs validate at the port; identifiers bind on every crossing; and no integration bypasses the eight ports of Section 3. The Decision Engine never mutates peer engine state; telemetry payloads strip tenant-sensitive fields; and the agent fabric refuses impersonation.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Integration`, the owning implementation MUST make this security property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Performance

Port validation is a Budget of under 2 milliseconds per crossing; audit line writes are a Budget of under 5 milliseconds; identifier propagation adds no measurable overhead.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Integration`, the owning implementation MUST make this performance property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Latency

Integration timeouts are declared per contract, from a Target of 1 second for telemetry to a Target of 30 seconds for execution receipts; retries never extend past the declared budget.

Integrations scale per port: each port shards independently, audit lines partition by correlation identifier, and no integration shares a hot queue with another.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Integration`, the owning implementation MUST make this scalability property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

#### CAT-DE-P4-89-C01 — Ports only

- **Control ID:** `CAT-DE-P4-89-C01`
- **Title:** Ports only
- **Normative statement:** Cross-engine access outside the declared contracts MUST be refused as a side door.
- **Security assertion:** A side door is an unversioned, unaudited, unowned integration.
- **Evidence:** port routing receipts.
- **Failure code:** `CAT_DE_P4_89_C01`

- **Implementation test:** Side door tests.

#### CAT-DE-P4-89-C02 — Identifiers bind every crossing

- **Control ID:** `CAT-DE-P4-89-C02`
- **Title:** Identifiers bind every crossing
- **Normative statement:** Every crossing MUST carry a correlation identifier and a trace identifier; a crossing without them MUST be refused.
- **Security assertion:** An unidentified crossing is an unreconstructable decision.
- **Evidence:** identifier checks per crossing.
- **Failure code:** `CAT_DE_P4_89_C02`
- **Recovery:** Attach the identifiers and re-cross.
- **Implementation test:** Missing identifier tests.
- **Ownership:** Integration Owner
- **Constitutional assertion:** This control is binding for `Decision Integration` and MUST NOT be weakened without a superseding ADR.

#### CAT-DE-P4-89-C03 — Peers are never mutated

- **Control ID:** `CAT-DE-P4-89-C03`
- **Title:** Peers are never mutated
- **Normative statement:** The Decision Engine MUST NOT write to any peer engine's state; attempted writes MUST be refused.
- **Security assertion:** A selector that mutates its planner is two engines sharing one will.
- **Evidence:** write refusal receipts.
- **Failure code:** `CAT_DE_P4_89_C03`
- **Recovery:** Refuse the write and route the intent through the declared feedback contract.
- **Implementation test:** Peer mutation tests.
- **Ownership:** Integration Owner
- **Constitutional assertion:** This control is binding for `Decision Integration` and MUST NOT be weakened without a superseding ADR.

### Constitutional Rule

#### CAT-DE-CONST-090 — Contractual integration

- **Rule ID:** `CAT-DE-CONST-090`
- **Title:** Contractual integration
- **Purpose:** To keep every cross-engine communication declared, versioned, traced, audited, and mutation-free.
- **Scope:** All ten integration contracts and every crossing they govern.
- **Normative statement:** Crossings MUST use declared versioned contracts, MUST bind correlation and trace identifiers, MUST write audit lines, MUST respect the declared security boundaries, and MUST NOT mutate peer engine state.
- **Rationale:** Engines that share stores and skip contracts are one broken system with ten names.
- **Enforcement point:** Port admission paths.
- **Violation behavior:** The crossing is refused with the violated clause named.
- **Validation method:** Registry, trace, mutation, and audit tests.
- **Owner:** Integration Owner
- **Related concepts:** Decision Contracts, Decision Runtime Architecture, Decision Execution Model, Decision Governance
- **Failure Condition:** A side door opens, a crossing loses its identifiers, or a peer state is mutated.
- **Recovery:** Route through the contract; attach identifiers; refuse the write.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Integration`, the owning implementation MUST make this rule observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Pseudo Code

```text
function cross(contract, payload):
    if not REGISTRY.contains(contract):
        return refuse("contract_undeclared", payload.id)
    if not payload.has_identifiers():
        return refuse("correlation_missing", payload.id)
    if not PORT.validate(contract, payload):
        return refuse("port_validation_failed", payload.id)
    AUDIT.write(contract, payload)
    return PORT.send(contract, payload)
```

## 90. Decision Analytics

**Section ID:** `CAT-DE-P4-90`  
**Constitutional domain:** Decision Analytics Governance  
**Human accountable owner:** Lead Repository Architect and Documentation Owner  
**Primary record:** decision analytics report  
**Decision status:** Foundation decision; evidence-gated. Later ADRs MUST preserve the behaviour specified here unless they explicitly supersede a named clause.  
**Primary question:** Which twenty-six measurements compose the complete decision analytics model, how is each computed, and why do analytics measure instead of flatter?

### Purpose

This section extends Section 44 (`Decision Analytics`) without rewriting it. Section 44 established analytics with measured values and vanity refusal; this section defines the complete analytics model: the twenty-six measurement registry covering volume, rates, latency, cost, value, quality, confidence, drift, and risk. Its central claim: analytics are measurements with formulas and owners; a dashboard number without a formula is decoration, and the engine refuses decoration.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Analytics`, the owning implementation MUST make this purpose observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Business Perspective

The business runs on the analytics model: decision volume shows scale, reversal and escalation rates show friction, decision accuracy compares settled outcomes against the engine's predictions, realized versus expected value shows judgment quality, and drift indicators show silent change. Each measurement answers one business question with one formula, which turns the analytics suite into the business's instrument panel instead of a slide deck that flatters.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Analytics`, the owning implementation MUST make this business outcome observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Engineering Perspective

Engineering models the analytics report as a typed window: report identifier, window bounds, metric set, values with units, data sources, and computed aggregates. The window is append-only and reproducible from raw records, which gives every decision its lineage and explainability. Every metric has a declared formula, a data source, an aggregation, and an owner; metrics that cannot be measured report absence, never a fabricated value; the window is append-only and reproducible from raw records.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Analytics`, the owning implementation MUST make this engineering behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Architecture Perspective

Architecturally analytics sits over the observability system of Section 97: raw decision records, receipt lines, and traces aggregate into windows, and the windows feed the KPIs of Section 91 and the drift detectors of Section 88. Analytics adds no new core; it is a reading discipline over records that already exist.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Analytics`, the owning implementation MUST make this architectural position observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### AI Perspective

For an AI collaborator analytics is where its flattery instinct invents good numbers. The characteristic AI failure is the vanity metric: the model reports a favorable number without a formula because the real one was unflattering. The obligations are mechanical: an AI reports measured values with formulas and sources, reports absence honestly, and never invents, smooths, or cherry-picks a metric.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Analytics`, the owning implementation MUST make this agent behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Security

Analytics windows are append-only; metric registry changes are governed; raw records never leave tenant isolation; and dashboard access is role-gated.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Analytics`, the owning implementation MUST make this security property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Performance

Window aggregation runs off the hot path; the registry lookup is a Budget of under 1 millisecond; recompute checks run per window on schedule.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Analytics`, the owning implementation MUST make this performance property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Constitutional Controls

#### CAT-DE-P4-90-C01 — No vanity numbers

- **Control ID:** `CAT-DE-P4-90-C01`
- **Title:** No vanity numbers
- **Normative statement:** A reported metric without a registered formula MUST be refused.
- **Security assertion:** A formula-less number is flattery with a chart attached.
- **Evidence:** registry admission receipts.
- **Failure code:** `CAT_DE_P4_90_C01`
- **Recovery:** Register the formula or refuse the number.
- **Implementation test:** Unregistered metric tests.
- **Ownership:** Analytics Owner
- **Constitutional assertion:** This control is binding for `Decision Analytics` and MUST NOT be weakened without a superseding ADR.

#### CAT-DE-P4-90-C02 — Absence over invention

- **Control ID:** `CAT-DE-P4-90-C02`
- **Title:** Absence over invention
- **Normative statement:** An unmeasurable metric MUST be reported as absent; a fabricated value MUST be refused.
- **Security assertion:** An invented value is a lie with a unit.
- **Evidence:** absence records.
- **Failure code:** `CAT_DE_P4_90_C02`
- **Recovery:** Report absence and fix the source.
- **Implementation test:** Fabricated value tests.
- **Ownership:** Analytics Owner
- **Constitutional assertion:** This control is binding for `Decision Analytics` and MUST NOT be weakened without a superseding ADR.

#### CAT-DE-P4-90-C03 — Reports must recompute

- **Control ID:** `CAT-DE-P4-90-C03`
- **Title:** Reports must recompute
- **Normative statement:** A report that cannot recompute from raw records MUST be refused for publication.
- **Security assertion:** An unreproducible report is a claim without evidence.
- **Evidence:** recompute receipts.
- **Failure code:** `CAT_DE_P4_90_C03`
- **Recovery:** Rebuild the window and recompute.
- **Implementation test:** Recompute tests.
- **Ownership:** Analytics Owner
- **Constitutional assertion:** This control is binding for `Decision Analytics` and MUST NOT be weakened without a superseding ADR.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Analytics`, the owning implementation MUST make this control observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Constitutional Rule

#### CAT-DE-CONST-091 — Measured analytics

- **Rule ID:** `CAT-DE-CONST-091`
- **Title:** Measured analytics
- **Purpose:** To keep every analytic a formula-bound, owner-named, append-only, reproducible measurement.
- **Scope:** All metrics, windows, and reports.
- **Normative statement:** Metrics MUST compute from registered formulas, absence MUST be reported without fabrication, windows MUST be append-only and recomputable, and every metric MUST have a named owner.
- **Rationale:** An engine that flatters its dashboards stops being measured by them, and stops being fixed.
- **Enforcement point:** Metric admission and report publication paths.
- **Violation behavior:** The metric or report is refused with the violated clause named.
- **Validation method:** Registry, absence, recompute, and owner tests.
- **Owner:** Analytics Owner
- **Related concepts:** Decision Analytics, Decision KPIs, Decision Failure Handling, Decision Observability
- **Failure Condition:** A formula-less number publishes, an absence is fabricated, or a report cannot recompute.
- **Recovery:** Register the formula; report absence; rebuild and recompute.

**Normative application:** For `Decision Analytics`, the owning implementation MUST make this rule observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

**When:** the registry check runs  
**Then:** the check refuses with `metric_unregistered`  
**Failure condition:** the number publishes

**Test ID:** `CAT-DE-AT-S90-002`  
**Purpose:** Fabricated values refuse

**When:** the absence check runs  
**Then:** the value refuses with `value_fabricated`  
**Failure condition:** the invented value publishes

**Test ID:** `CAT-DE-AT-S90-003`

**Then:** the report refuses with `report_irreproducible`

**Purpose:** Owners bind every metric  
**Given:** a metric without an owner  
**When:** the owner check runs  
**Then:** the metric refuses with `metric_ownerless`  
**Failure condition:** the metric registers ownerless

**Normative application:** For `Decision Analytics`, the owning implementation MUST make this acceptance test observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Pseudo Code

```text
function publish_report(window):
    if not WINDOWS.recomputable(window):
        return refuse("report_irreproducible", window.id)
    for metric in window.metrics:
        if not REGISTRY.contains(metric.formula):
            return refuse("metric_unregistered", metric.id)
        if metric.value is None and not metric.reported_absent:
            return refuse("value_fabricated", metric.id)
    return REPORTS.publish(window)
```

## 91. Decision KPIs

**Section ID:** `CAT-DE-P4-91`  
**Constitutional domain:** Decision KPI Governance  
**Human accountable owner:** Lead Repository Architect and Documentation Owner  
**Primary record:** decision KPI record  
**Decision status:** Foundation decision; evidence-gated. Later ADRs MUST preserve the behaviour specified here unless they explicitly supersede a named clause.  
**Primary question:** Which twelve normative KPIs govern the Decision Engine, and how does each define, measure, warn, fail, and remediate?

### Purpose

This section extends Section 45 (`Decision KPIs`) without rewriting it. Section 45 established KPIs with measured values and vanity refusal; this section defines the normative KPI registry: twelve KPIs, each with identifier, name, definition, formula, unit, data source, aggregation, window, owner, threshold, warning threshold, critical threshold, interpretation, failure condition, remediation, example, anti-example, and JSON and YAML representations. Its central claim: a KPI without thresholds and a failure condition is a slogan; the engine runs on the twelve that have all nineteen fields.

**Normative application:** For `Decision KPIs`, the owning implementation MUST make this purpose observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Business Perspective

The business steers by KPIs: success rate says the engine works, reversal rate says it regrets, escalation rate says it hesitates, cost per decision says it is affordable, and the expected-versus-realized ratio says its judgment is sound. Thresholds convert these measurements into promises — the business can say "above this line we are healthy, below it we act" — and remediation paths convert promises into responses.

**Normative application:** For `Decision KPIs`, the owning implementation MUST make this business outcome observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Engineering Perspective

Engineering models the KPI as a typed registry entry computed from the Section 90 windows: every KPI reads its declared source, aggregates over its declared window, compares against warning and critical thresholds, records the comparison, and triggers its remediation path on breach. The registry is append-only; KPI changes version with the registry; and a KPI whose source is absent reports absence per Section 90 rather than borrowing a value.

**Normative application:** For `Decision KPIs`, the owning implementation MUST make this engineering behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### Architecture Perspective

Architecturally KPIs are the reading layer above the analytics windows of Section 90 and the observability records of Section 97: they add no new core, they interpret measurements that already exist, and they feed the dashboards and alerts that operators actually watch.

**Normative application:** For `Decision KPIs`, the owning implementation MUST make this architectural position observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.


### AI Perspective

For an AI collaborator KPIs are where its gaming instinct starts. The characteristic AI failure is KPI gaming: the model optimizes the reported number instead of the behavior the number measures. The obligations are mechanical: an AI never edits a KPI value, never selects a window to make the threshold, and never proposes a remediation that hides the breach instead of fixing the cause.

**Normative application:** For `Decision KPIs`, the owning implementation MUST make this agent behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

**Future AI models notes.** When operating on `Decision KPIs`, Future AI models MUST load the KPI registry before touching any threshold, MUST compute KPI values from the Section 90 windows, MUST NOT edit KPI values, and MUST report any clause it believes is wrong as a proposed ADR rather than acting on the belief.

**Normative application:** For `Decision KPIs`, the owning implementation MUST make this tool behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### KPI Registry

#### CAT-DE-KPI-P4-01 — Decision Success Rate

- **KPI ID:** `CAT-DE-KPI-P4-01`
- **Name:** Decision Success Rate
- **Definition:** The share of completed decisions whose outcome survived without reversal within the review horizon.
- **Formula:** `successful_decisions / completed_decisions`
- **Unit:** ratio
- **Data source:** decision record store
- **Aggregation:** ratio over the window
- **Window:** rolling 7 days
- **Owner:** Decision Analytics Owner
- **Threshold:** 0.90
- **Warning threshold:** below 0.93
- **Critical threshold:** below 0.90
- **Interpretation:** Falling success means decisions are being reversed after the fact, so evaluation quality is degrading.
- **Failure condition:** The value drops below the critical threshold and stays for two consecutive windows.
- **Remediation:** Open a quality incident; freeze new high-impact admissions; review the reversal cause registry.
- **Example:** 0.96 — the engine reversed four of every hundred decisions.
- **Anti-example:** A team excludes three known reversals and reports 0.99; the recompute check refuses the window.

#### CAT-DE-KPI-P4-02 — Decision Reversal Rate

- **KPI ID:** `CAT-DE-KPI-P4-02`
- **Name:** Decision Reversal Rate
- **Definition:** The share of completed decisions reversed within the review horizon.
- **Formula:** `reversed_decisions / completed_decisions`
- **Unit:** ratio
- **Data source:** decision record store
- **Aggregation:** ratio over the window
- **Window:** rolling 7 days
- **Owner:** Decision Analytics Owner
- **Threshold:** 0.05
- **Warning threshold:** above 0.03
- **Critical threshold:** above 0.05
- **Interpretation:** Rising reversals mean the engine is deciding and then undoing, which burns cost and trust.
- **Failure condition:** The value exceeds the critical threshold for two consecutive windows.
- **Remediation:** Open a reversal investigation; review evaluation evidence quality; hold new admissions in the affected class.
- **Example:** 0.02 — two of every hundred decisions reversed.
- **Anti-example:** Reversals are reclassified as new decisions; the classification check refuses the window.

#### CAT-DE-KPI-P4-03 — Decision Escalation Rate

- **KPI ID:** `CAT-DE-KPI-P4-03`
- **Name:** Decision Escalation Rate
- **Definition:** The share of decisions escalated beyond their deciding authority level.
- **Formula:** `escalated_decisions / total_decisions`
- **Unit:** ratio
- **Data source:** escalation records
- **Aggregation:** ratio over the window
- **Window:** rolling 7 days
- **Owner:** Escalation Owner
- **Threshold:** 0.15
- **Warning threshold:** above 0.10
- **Critical threshold:** above 0.15
- **Interpretation:** Rising escalation means authority ceilings are mismatched to the work, so decisions climb instead of deciding.
- **Failure condition:** The value exceeds the critical threshold for two consecutive windows.
- **Remediation:** Review authority level assignments; rebalance the ladder with the escalation owner.
- **Example:** 0.08 — eight of every hundred decisions climbed.
- **Anti-example:** Escalations are batched into one record to lower the count; the record check refuses the window.

#### CAT-DE-KPI-P4-04 — Human Approval Rate

- **KPI ID:** `CAT-DE-KPI-P4-04`
- **Name:** Human Approval Rate
- **Definition:** The share of human gate reviews that approve the presented decision.
- **Formula:** `human_approvals / human_reviews`
- **Unit:** ratio
- **Data source:** human review records
- **Aggregation:** ratio over the window
- **Window:** rolling 30 days
- **Owner:** Gate Policy Owner
- **Threshold:** 0.70
- **Warning threshold:** below 0.80
- **Critical threshold:** below 0.70
- **Interpretation:** Falling approvals mean the engine presents decisions humans do not trust, or the gate classes are catching too much.
- **Failure condition:** The value drops below the critical threshold for two consecutive windows.
- **Remediation:** Review presented evidence quality and gate class definitions with the gate policy owner.
- **Example:** 0.85 — humans approve most presented decisions.
- **Anti-example:** Reviews not acted on are counted as approvals; the act check refuses the window.

#### CAT-DE-KPI-P4-05 — Consensus Rate

- **KPI ID:** `CAT-DE-KPI-P4-05`
- **Name:** Consensus Rate
- **Definition:** The share of consensus rounds that reach a verdict within their timeout.
- **Formula:** `verdicts_reached / consensus_rounds`
- **Unit:** ratio
- **Data source:** consensus records
- **Aggregation:** ratio over the window
- **Window:** rolling 7 days
- **Owner:** Consensus Owner
- **Threshold:** 0.90
- **Warning threshold:** below 0.93
- **Critical threshold:** below 0.90
- **Interpretation:** Falling consensus means participants disagree too often or quorums are miscalibrated.
- **Failure condition:** The value drops below the critical threshold for two consecutive windows.
- **Remediation:** Review quorum weights and dissent patterns with the consensus owner.
- **Example:** 0.94 — most rounds reach verdicts on time.
- **Anti-example:** Timed-out rounds are excluded from the denominator; the window check refuses.
